```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
Sys.setenv(OMP_NUM_THREADS = "1")
```

PaPeR assigns genotyped parents (a dam and a sire) to genotyped individuals,
from microhaplotype or SNP genotypes plus each individual's sex and birth year.
This vignette walks through a full analysis of the simulated example data that
ships with the package, then shows how to prepare your own data.

PaPeR is inspired by the parentage step of
[Sequoia](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=sequoia) (Huisman 2017) and uses
the same kind of inputs and settings, so Sequoia users will find most of it
familiar. The last section lists the settings side by side.

```{r setup}
library(PaPeR)
```

## The example data

`pap_example` is a simulated population with overlapping generations: 150
founders born in 2015 and 110 offspring a year from 2016 to 2020. 595 of the
700 individuals are genotyped, once on 100 microhaplotypes (3 to 8 alleles per
locus) and once on 150 SNPs. The true pedigree is included so we can check
the results.

```{r data}
ex <- pap_example
dim(ex$GenoM)
ex$GenoM[1:4, 1:6]
head(ex$LifeHistData, 4)
```

Genotypes are character calls `"a/b"`, where `a` and `b` are allele numbers
`1, 2, ..., k` at that locus and `"0"` marks a missing call. Row names are the
individual IDs. `LifeHistData` follows Sequoia's format: `ID`, `Sex` (1 female,
2 male, 3 or `NA` unknown) and `BirthYear`, optionally with `BY.min`, `BY.max`
and `Year.last`.

## Check the markers

`MHStats()` is the multiallelic counterpart of Sequoia's `SnpStats()`. It
reports allele frequencies, call rates, the effective number of alleles (`Ae`)
and the polymorphic information content (PIC) of every locus.

```{r stats}
st <- MHStats(ex$GenoM, warn_Ae = 0)
head(st$ALL[, c("locus", "call_rate", "n_alleles", "Ae", "PIC")])
summary(st$ALL$Ae)
```

## Check for duplicate samples

PaPeR assumes each individual was sampled once, so remove duplicate samples
first. `find_duplicates()` scores every pair of samples as "the same
individual" against unrelated and against close relatives. Here we add a
second copy of one sample to the first 60 individuals:

```{r duplicates}
G <- ex$GenoM[1:60, ]
G <- rbind(G, resampled = G["ID0012", ])
dups <- find_duplicates(G, Dropout = 0.005, Foreign = 5e-4, thresh = 5)
dups[, c("ID1", "ID2", "LLR", "LLR_MZ_vs_best", "best_other_relationship",
         "jointly_called", "mismatch_rate")]
```

The duplicate is found with a large LLR, and "same individual" beats the best
alternative (full siblings) by a wide margin. `find_duplicates()` compares every
pair of samples, so on thousands of samples it takes a while.

## Assign parents

`assign_parents()` takes the genotypes, the life history and two error rates
for microhaplotypes:

- `Dropout`: the probability that a true heterozygote is called as one of its
  homozygotes;
- `Foreign`: the probability that an allele copy is replaced by a random
  allele from the population.

Starting values are enough. By default PaPeR re-estimates the error rate from
the confident parent-offspring trios it finds and, if the data show more
errors than you assumed, raises it and searches again.

```{r assign}
ped <- assign_parents(ex$GenoM, ex$LifeHistData,
                      Dropout = 0.005, Foreign = 5e-4,
                      control = list(CalcLLR = TRUE))
head(ped[!is.na(ped$dam), c("id", "dam", "sire", "LLRdam", "LLRsire",
                            "LLRpair", "OHdam", "OHsire", "MEpair")])
```

The output has one row per genotyped individual. `dam` and `sire` are `NA`
where no genotyped parent was found. With `CalcLLR = TRUE` it also has
Sequoia-style columns:

- `LLRdam`, `LLRsire`: base-10 log-likelihood ratio of each assigned parent
  against the best non-parent relationship, with the other parent kept;
- `LLRpair`: the weaker of the two when both are assigned;
- `OHdam`, `OHsire`: opposite homozygotes, loci where parent and offspring
  share no allele;
- `MEpair`: Mendelian errors in the trio.

The calibration record shows the error rate used in each search, the rate
fitted from the confident trios with its 95% interval, and the decision:

```{r calibration}
attr(ped, "calibration")
```

Here the supplied dropout rate (0.005) lies inside the fitted interval, so
PaPeR kept it and needed only one search.

### How good is it?

Because the data are simulated we can compare with the truth.
`score_pedigree()` counts correct, wrong and missed parents. With `typed_ids`,
a true parent that was never genotyped counts as "no parent", so assigning
anyone to that slot counts as wrong.

```{r score}
sc <- score_pedigree(ped, ex$Pedigree, typed_ids = rownames(ex$GenoM))
sapply(sc, function(x) unlist(x[c("assigned", "correct", "wrong", "missed")]))
```

Every genotyped parent is found, and no parent is assigned where the true
parent was not genotyped.

## SNP data

SNPs use the same genotype format with alleles 1 and 2. For SNP panels you can
use Sequoia's error model, with a single error rate `Err`:

```{r snp}
ped_snp <- assign_parents(ex$GenoM_snp, ex$LifeHistData,
                          control = list(error_model = "sequoia", Err = 0.005))
sc_snp <- score_pedigree(ped_snp, ex$Pedigree, typed_ids = rownames(ex$GenoM))
sapply(sc_snp, function(x) unlist(x[c("assigned", "correct", "wrong", "missed")]))
```

150 SNPs carry less information than 100 microhaplotypes, so a few parents
are missed and one is wrong. That difference is the reason to use
microhaplotypes.

## Preparing your own data

### SNPs in Sequoia format

Sequoia stores SNP genotypes as a numeric matrix of 0, 1 and 2 copies, with
negative numbers for missing calls. PaPeR does not accept numeric matrices,
because the same numbers could mean allele codes. Convert them first:

```{r convert-snp}
sequoia_to_pap <- function(G) {
  out <- matrix("0", nrow(G), ncol(G), dimnames = dimnames(G))
  ok <- !is.na(G) & G >= 0
  out[ok] <- c("1/1", "1/2", "2/2")[G[ok] + 1]
  out
}
G012 <- matrix(c(0, 1, 2, -9, 1, 0), nrow = 2,
               dimnames = list(c("A", "B"), c("snp1", "snp2", "snp3")))
sequoia_to_pap(G012)
```

### Microhaplotype allele codes

Allele numbers must run from 1 to the number of alleles at each locus. If your
genotype caller writes allele names (for example haplotype sequences) or
larger numbers such as `101/103`, recode each locus first. PaPeR takes the
largest number it sees as the number of alleles at that locus, so codes in the
hundreds make huge likelihood tables and a very slow run.

```{r recode}
recode_alleles <- function(G) {
  for (l in seq_len(ncol(G))) {
    called <- G[, l] != "0"
    ab <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(G[called, l], "/", fixed = TRUE))
    lev <- sort(unique(as.vector(ab)))
    a <- match(ab[, 1], lev)
    b <- match(ab[, 2], lev)
    G[called, l] <- paste0(pmin(a, b), "/", pmax(a, b))
  }
  G
}
raw <- matrix(c("101/103", "103/103", "0", "101/214"), ncol = 1,
              dimnames = list(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), "locus1"))
cbind(original = raw[, 1], recoded = recode_alleles(raw)[, 1])
```

### Life history

- Every genotyped individual needs a `BirthYear`, or both `BY.min` and
  `BY.max` when the exact year is uncertain. Give a range rather than a guess:
  a wrong exact year can rule out the true parent.
- Sequoia uses negative numbers for unknown values. Set them to `NA` for
  PaPeR.
- IDs must match the genotype row names exactly, so check for stray spaces
  (`trimws()`) and numbers stored as text.

```{r lifehist, eval = FALSE}
LH <- LifeHistData
for (col in intersect(c("BirthYear", "BY.min", "BY.max", "Year.last"), names(LH)))
  LH[[col]][!is.na(LH[[col]]) & LH[[col]] < 0] <- NA
LH$ID <- trimws(as.character(LH$ID))
```

## Settings for Sequoia users

Everything beyond the genotypes, life history and error rates goes in
`control`; `pap_control()` lists every setting with its default and rejects
unknown names.

| Sequoia | PaPeR (`control = list(...)`) | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `Err` | `error_model = "sequoia", Err = ...` (SNPs) or `Dropout`, `Foreign` arguments | dropout/foreign model |
| `Tassign` | `Tassign` | 0.5 |
| `Tfilter` | `Tfilter` | -2 |
| `args.AP = list(MinAgeParent, MaxAgeParent)` | `MinAgeParent`, `MaxAgeParent` | 1; span of birth years |
| `CalcLLR` | `CalcLLR` | `FALSE` |
| (no equivalent) | `error_calibration`: `"raise_guarded"`, `"raise_only"` or `"none"` | `"raise_guarded"` |
| `SnpStats()` | `MHStats()` | |
| `GetMaybeRel()` | `get_maybe_rel()` | |
| `CalcOHLLR()` | `calc_llr()` | |
| `CalcPairLL()` | `calc_pair_LL()`, `calc_trio_LL()` | |

Sibship clustering and dummy parents (Sequoia's `Module = "ped"`) are outside
PaPeR's scope: it assigns genotyped parents only.

## Learn more

- `?assign_parents` and `?pap_control` document every argument and setting.
- The model, error models and calibration are described in `docs/model.md`
  in the [source repository](https://github.com/ty-wittman/PaPeR).

## Reference

Huisman, J. (2017). Pedigree reconstruction from SNP data: parentage
assignment, sibship clustering and beyond. *Molecular Ecology Resources*,
17(5), 1009–1024. <https://doi.org/10.1111/1755-0998.12665>
